title: Fake news and covid-19 in Italy: Results of a quantitative observational study
screen_reason: Content analysis of 2,102 Italian-language COVID-19 article links retrieved from BuzzSumo (9 keyword pairs x 3 periods), each independently coded by two authors as fake or science-based. Table 3 reports both the share of reviewed articles classified fake (31.9%) and the share of all shares that went to fake articles (23.1%), each against a stated denominator. That gives a CONTENT estimate and a SHARING (content_share) estimate.

estimates.platform: BuzzSumo aggregation of most-shared links across Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit and Twitter
estimates.measure_type: % of reviewed COVID-19 article links classified as fake news (vs science-based)
estimates.denominator: All retained reviewed article links from the 27 BuzzSumo searches (fake + science-based); the paper states 2,102 articles were reviewed and each search was stopped at 100 articles counting fake + science-based
estimates.definition: Article coded fake if its content was not supported by scientific literature, or if the data reported were used to draw inappropriate conclusions about SARS-CoV-2; articles merely reporting on fake claims while flagging them as unevidenced were included in the review; non-health/non-science content (e.g. socioeconomic coverage) was excluded before coding.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Articles were classified as fake news if the content was not supported by scientific literature or when the data reported were used to make inappropriate conclusions about SARS-CoV-2."
estimates.source_quote: Key Words           No. News (%)          No. Shares (%) Italian (English)     Fake     Verified     Fake      Verified Vitamina C (vitamin C)     24.0%     76.0%       32.0%       68.0% Vitamina D (vitamin D)     79.6%     20.4%       89.4%       10.6% Aglio (garlic)        18.0%     82.0%       68.4%       31.6% 5G (5G)            32.8%     67.2%       36.8%       63.2% Vaccino (vaccine)        7.7%     92.7%        6.6%       93.4% Complotto (plot)        29.3%     70.7%       27.7%       72.3% Origine (origin)       37.3%     62.7%       14.8%       85.2% Laboratorio (laboratory)   52.8%     47.2%       65.6%       34.4% HIV (HIV)            11.1%     88.9%       77.8%       22.2% Total             31.9%     68.1%       23.1%       76.9%
estimates.page_loc: Table 3, p. 7 (Results, p. 5: "Overall, we reviewed 2102 articles")
estimates.ground_truth_detail: "Each link was independently reviewed by two of the authors. In case of disagreement between the authors, a third author was involved in the review." Coders were the study's own public-health researchers; criterion was support in the scientific literature; no kappa or agreement statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The search bars we applied always contained the word "coronavirus" and one other specific associated term ... The keywords were chosen according to the most frequent topics of the "fake news" that spread during the Covid-19 pandemic. ... We concluded each search when all of the findings were examined or once we had reviewed 100 articles by adding the number of false articles to the number of science-based articles.
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated on two grounds: the keyword set was deliberately chosen to surface fake news ('the most likely to uncover health-related false information'), and BuzzSumo returns MOST-SHARED links truncated at 100 per search. This inflates the estimate relative to a random sample of COVID-19 coverage. Denominator ambiguity: 2,102 is described as the number of articles 'reviewed', while the Table 3 percentages are shares of (fake + verified) after exclusions, whose count is not reported - hence medium confidence.

estimates.platform: BuzzSumo aggregation of shares/engagement across Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit and Twitter
estimates.measure_type: % of all shares of the reviewed COVID-19 links that went to links containing fake news
estimates.value_raw: Links that contained fake news were shared 2,352,585 times, accounting for 23.1% of the total shares of all the articles reviewed (Table 3 Total: Fake 23.1% / Verified 76.9%)
estimates.denominator: All shares of the reviewed article links (fake + science-based) across Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit and Twitter; only the fake-news share count (2,352,585) and the percentage are reported, the grand total of shares is not printed
estimates.definition: A share counted toward the numerator if it was a share/engagement of a link coded as fake news (content unsupported by scientific literature or drawing inappropriate conclusions about SARS-CoV-2).
estimates.misinfo_def: "Articles were classified as fake news if the content was not supported by scientific literature or when the data reported were used to make inappropriate conclusions about SARS-CoV-2."
estimates.n: 2,352,585 shares of fake-news links out of all shares of the 2,102 reviewed articles
estimates.source_quote: Altogether throughout the three periods, links that contained untrue information were shared 2,352,585 times, accounting for about 23.1% of the total shares of all the articles reviewed.
estimates.page_loc: Results p. 5 and Abstract; Table 3 Total row, p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two of the authors independently reviewed each link, a third adjudicated disagreements; criterion was support in the scientific literature; no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: BuzzSumo gathers data across the social media platforms Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit, and Twitter to generate a list of article links with the highest online engagement. Engagement is defined as the total number of interactions that users have with a particular article link, including actions such as "liking", "commenting", and "sharing" on social media.
estimates.notes: SHARING rather than CONTENT because the denominator is share/engagement counts, not items (governing rule in section 3). The paper's 'shares' are BuzzSumo engagement counts (likes + comments + shares), so the label is looser than a pure reshare count - a judgement call worth adjudicator attention. The corpus was selected as the MOST-SHARED links, so this is not a random sample of Italian COVID sharing.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) NOT extracted as separate rows: the nine keyword-level rows of Table 3, which are topical sub-corpora of the same searches rather than separate countries/platforms/measures. Verbatim, News% fake / Shares% fake: vitamin C 24.0% / 32.0%; vitamin D 79.6% / 89.4%; garlic 18.0% / 68.4%; 5G 32.8% / 36.8%; vaccine 7.7% / 6.6%; plot 29.3% / 27.7%; origin 37.3% / 14.8%; laboratory 52.8% / 65.6%; HIV 11.1% / 77.8%. If the review splits by topic, these 18 values are available. (2) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES the adjudicator should see: the Results text says "The topics most contaminated with fakes were vitamin D (89.4%), HIV (77.8%), and garlic (71.2%)" but Table 3 gives garlic shares as 68.4%; the Discussion instead says garlic fake links accounted for "almost 70% of the shares"; and the Table 3 vaccine row reads 7.7% fake / 92.7% verified, which sums to 100.4%. (3) Raw per-search counts are given only in prose for a few cells (e.g. HIV: 1 fake article/767 shares in period 1, 15 fake articles/72,715 shares in period 3; laboratory: 55 fake articles/1,039,224 shares in period 1) - these are counts without their own denominators, so no rows. (4) Time series were collapsed to the single all-period Total row per the protocol; Figure 1 is unreadable in the text extraction. (5) Prevalence figures quoted from other studies (82% of Italians cannot recognise fake information; health-literacy percentages) are citations to elsewhere and are excluded by R8. (6) The number of excluded articles is never reported, so the exact denominator behind 31.9% cannot be reconstructed.

rob.design: Observational content analysis using BuzzSumo's most-shared-link search: 9 two-keyword Italian queries (coronavirus + vaccine/origin/laboratory/plot/HIV/vitamin C/vitamin D/garlic/5G), each run over 3 date ranges spanning 31 Dec 2019 - 30 Apr 2020 = 27 searches, Italian-language filter; each search terminated when all findings were examined or at 100 articles (fake + science-based); 2,102 articles reviewed; every link independently reviewed by two of the authors with a third author adjudicating disagreements, but NO inter-coder reliability statistic reported; keyword set deliberately chosen to surface fake news and non-health/non-science items excluded, so the sampling frame is purposively enriched for misinformation; engagement counts come from a third-party commercial tool (free 7-day trial), platform coverage limited to Facebook, Pinterest, Reddit, Twitter; no funding, no ethics issue.
rob.item6_quote: Articles were classified as fake news if the content was not supported by scientific literature or when the data reported were used to make inappropriate conclusions about SARS-CoV-2.
rob.item10_quote: Altogether throughout the three periods, links that contained untrue information were shared 2,352,585 times, accounting for about 23.1% of the total shares of all the articles reviewed.
